claims.claim: Hong Kong should not impose a hard cap on initial rents for subdivided units.
Tenure security and standards should be tightened instead, paired with a light, reviewable rent band.
A hard cap would bind hardest on the households it claims to protect.
The actual pain point for tenants is the queue and insecurity, not the rent level.
SDU tenants are disproportionately new arrivals, single-parent households, and public-housing waiters facing a queue of about five and a half years.
Mr Chan would accept any rent if the public-housing queue were three years instead of five and a half.
61 percent of surveyed households would trade a nominal rent increase for three-year tenure security.
74 percent of surveyed households would trade a nominal rent increase for a faster public-housing offer.
A rent cap addresses the price symptom of a quantity problem.
The long-run elasticity of SDU-type supply is estimated at 0.31 to 0.48.
A 10 percent cap-induced rent reduction removes roughly 3 to 5 percent of stock over five years.
A 15 percent cut in initial rents transfers about 900 dollars a month to incumbents while 3,000 to 4,000 households a year cannot enter the segment.
The 2021 Tenancy Control Ordinance capped increases within tenancies but not initial rents.
Estimated SDU stock rose from 100,800 units in 2019 to 111,200 in 2025.
First-generation rent controls show consistent supply contraction, while second-generation controls show small or null effects.
The 2021 ordinance's stability is an artifact of a non-binding instrument.
Real rent burden worsened from 31 to 34 percent.
Berlin's 2020 rent cap cut initial-offer rents sharply but supply contracted within a year.
When Berlin's cap was lifted, suppressed increases released above the pre-cap trend.
Rent caps bind differently on new entrants than incumbents, protecting those already inside and handing the bill to those still outside.
Inspection capacity covers under 6 percent of stock per year.
A band-based cap would need a certifiable tenancy register costing 40 to 60 staff-years.
Enforcement would systematically miss the most exploited tail, including tenants with no written agreement and the newest arrivals.
The recommended alternative is a published, indexed per-square-foot rent band combined with tenure security.
Enforcement spending should focus on fire, partition, and ventilation hazards.

[0] (typed) I'm trying to get a handle on Hong Kong's subdivided flats and the housing policy debate around them. Could you pull up some sources on that topic for me?
[2] (typed) I want to start broad and just see what's out there on subdivided units in Hong Kong — the basic descriptive picture of who lives in them and why. Could you pull up something that gives an overview of the tenants and the housing situation?
[4] (typed) It's for an essay where I want to set up who ends up in subdivided units and why they're there in the first place. I don't have a claim yet — I just want a source that gives me the profile of these tenants and the broader housing context they're stuck in. Something descriptive to anchor the opening.
[6] (pick reason) descriptive overview plus first-hand tenant account to anchor the opening
[20] (typed) Thanks. Before I go further, I want to understand the household profile behind these units and what tenants themselves say the real problem is. Can you pull a document that surveys SDU tenants at scale — something with numbers on what they'd trade for security or a faster housing offer — and one that lays out the supply picture and any elasticity estimates? I've only looked at the primer and the interview so far.
[22] (typed) Fair. Let me be more concrete. For the tenant-side piece I want something that quantifies what households would accept in exchange for security or a faster offer — a survey with percentages. For the supply side I want elasticity estimates, ideally a range, so I can see how responsive this kind of stock is to rent. And honestly I keep circling back to the interview I already have — the tenant who talks about the waiting list — because I want to test whether his framing is idiosyncratic or representative. So: one survey document with trade-off numbers, and one document carrying supply elasticity, please.
[24] (pick reason) survey trade-offs, supply elasticity, and stock data for tenant-side and supply-side claims
[26] (pick reason) tenant trade-off survey and supply elasticity paper
[40] (pick reason) Berlin case study needed for comparative evidence
[45] (typed) I still need the Hong Kong enforcement and legal material to round out the picture — the inspection capacity and the legal opinion on instruments. Can you surface sources on those?
[47] (typed) The inspection-capacity piece is meant to support a practical objection: that a tightened cap could not actually be enforced across the stock. The legal opinion is meant to show what instrument a careful lawyer thinks is defensible instead. For the first I'd need evidence of how much of the stock inspectors actually reach; for the second, a definition of the instruments and their legal footing.
[49] (pick reason) Enforcement capacity and legal instrument footing
[62] (typed) I think I've got what I need from those two. Let me pull the remaining thread together — I want to check one last source before I try to write anything, something that speaks to the landlord side and the actual margin economics, since I keep hearing that owners can't absorb anything.
[64] (typed) Something with the landlord's own account would be ideal — someone who actually owns and lets these units, saying in plain terms what they can and can't absorb, so I can test the claim that owners can't take any cut at all against a real voice rather than a slogan.
